blocks.html:
William Shakespeare was a prolific writer in the Elizabethan and Jacobean ages. He is famous for his plays, sonnets and other poems. The textbook reminds us that his works continue to shape English literature across the world.

This extract from As You Like It is one of his most quoted speeches. In it, Shakespeare compares the world to a stage and human life to a play with seven ages.

blocks.label: Why this poem matters
blocks.text: The poem gives a clear picture of human life from birth to old age. It is both simple and deep, because it turns ordinary stages of life into dramatic scenes.

blocks.html:
The warm up shows the life cycle of a butterfly and asks students to think about the stages of human growth from a newborn to an adult. That idea fits the poem perfectly, because Shakespeare also sees life as a series of stages.

The textbook gives age-group words such as denarian, vicenarian, tricenarian and so on. These help us see that age itself can be thought of as a sequence.

blocks.quote: All the world's a stage, / And all the men and women merely players;

blocks.label: Before you read
blocks.text: The poem does not talk only about theatre. It uses theatre to explain life itself.

blocks.quote:
At first the infant,
Mewling and puking in the nurse's arms;

blocks.html: The infant depends completely on the nurse. It cries and vomits, showing weakness and helplessness. Shakespeare starts with the very beginning of life.

blocks.quote:
Then the whining school-boy, with his satchel
And shining morning face, creeping like snail
Unwillingly to school.

blocks.html: The school-boy is unwilling to go to school. His slow movement and unhappy face show that childhood has its own reluctance and routine.

blocks.quote:
And then the lover,
Sighing like furnace, with a woeful ballad
Made to his mistress' eyebrow.

blocks.html: The lover is full of passion and longing. He writes songs and sighs deeply. Shakespeare presents youth as emotional and intense.

blocks.quote:
Then a soldier,
Full of strange oaths, and bearded like the pard,
Jealous in honour, sudden and quick in quarrel,
Seeking the bubble reputation
Even in the cannon's mouth.

blocks.html: The soldier is brave, proud and quick to fight. He seeks reputation even in danger. Shakespeare shows the energy and recklessness of this stage.

blocks.quote:
And then the justice,
In fair round belly with good capon lin'd,
With eyes severe and beard of formal cut,
Full of wise saws and modern instances;

blocks.html: The justice is mature, calm and wise. He is respected, fuller-bodied and more measured. Shakespeare links age with judgement and experience.
The old man becomes thin, weak and dependent. He uses spectacles and walks slowly. His voice also begins to fail.

blocks.quote:
Last scene of all,
That ends this strange eventful history,
Is second childishness and mere oblivion;
Sans teeth, sans eyes, sans taste, sans everything.

blocks.html: The final stage is old age at its weakest. It becomes like childhood again, but this time with loss and oblivion. Shakespeare ends by showing how life completes its own cycle.

blocks.label: Big idea
blocks.text: The poem makes us see life as a journey through seven roles. Each role has its own mood, strength and weakness.

blocks.html: These lines express the main thought of the poem and should be remembered for revision.

blocks.html: Shakespeare compares life to a stage and people to actors. Everyone enters and exits, and everyone plays different roles.

blocks.text: Theme: The seven ages of man

blocks.html: The poem traces birth, childhood, youth, maturity, old age and second childhood. It shows that life is a movement from dependence to strength and back to dependence again.
Time changes everything. Strength fades, the voice weakens and the senses slowly disappear.

blocks.exp: The whole poem is built on the metaphor of life as theatre.
The school-boy is compared to a snail.
The soldier is compared to a leopard.
The repeated starting sound gives musical force.

blocks.exp: The line creates a vivid picture of total loss in old age.

blocks.html:
1. Short answers

a) What is the world compared to?
The world is compared to a stage.

b) What do the words "exits" and "entrances" mean?
They mean death and birth or leaving and entering the stage of life.

c) What is the first stage of a human's life?
The infant is the first stage.

d) Describe the second stage of life.
It is the whining school-boy stage, where the boy goes unwillingly to school.

e) How does a man play a lover's role?
He sighs, writes ballads and is full of passionate feeling.

f) Bring out the features of the fourth stage of a man.
The soldier is brave, quick in quarrel, full of oaths and eager for reputation.

g) When does a man become a judge? How?
In maturity, when he becomes wise, serious and respected.

h) Which stage is associated with the "shrunk shank"?
The sixth stage, the lean and slipper'd pantaloon.

i) Why is the last stage called second childishness?
Because old age makes a person helpless again, like a child.

2. Explain briefly

a) "They have their exits and their entrances; And one man in his time plays many parts."
People enter life at birth and exit at death. During life, each person plays many roles at different ages.

b) "Jealous in honour, sudden and quick in quarrel, Seeking the bubble reputation."
The soldier is proud, easily provoked and eager for fame, even if the fame is short-lived.

c) "Is second childishness and mere oblivion; Sans teeth, sans eyes, sans taste, sans everything."
The final stage is old age, when the person loses strength, senses and memory and becomes completely dependent.

3. Figures of speech

a) "All the world's a stage"
Metaphor.

b) "And all the men and women merely players"
Metaphor.

c) "And shining morning face, creeping like snail"
Simile.

d) "Full of strange oaths, and bearded like the pard"
Simile.

e) "Seeking the bubble reputation"
Metaphor.

f) "His youthful hose, well sav'd, a world too wide"
Hyperbole and imagery.

g) "and his big manly voice, turning again toward childish treble"
Imagery and contrast.

4. Alliteration

a) and all the men and women merely players
m sound.

b) And one man in his time plays many parts
m sound.

c) Jealous in honour, sudden and quick in quarrel
q sound.

5. Reference extracts

School-boy extract - The boy is unwilling to go to school, creeps like a snail and carries a satchel. He is slow, reluctant and very young.

Soldier extract - The soldier is full of strange oaths, quick in quarrel and eager for reputation. He is brave but reckless.

Justice extract - The justice is round-bellied, severe-eyed and wise. He speaks with knowledge and authority.

Completed summary: Shakespeare views the whole world as a stage where men and women are merely players. They enter the stage when they are born and leave it when they die. A man plays seven roles during his lifetime. As an infant, he depends fully on his mother or nurse. Then he becomes a school-boy, unwilling to go to school. Next he plays the lover who sighs for his beloved. In the fourth stage, he becomes a soldier who seeks reputation. In the fifth, he turns into a judge with wisdom and experience. During the sixth stage, he becomes old, weak and dependent. In the last stage, he becomes like a child again and loses his senses. Thus, life is a journey from helplessness to maturity and back to helplessness.

The textbook asks students to explain lines about the school-boy, the soldier and the justice, and to answer questions about the world, exits, entrances, figure of speech and alliteration. These answers are already summarized in the Q&A tab.
The speaking task asks students to discuss the roles and responsibilities of the second stage of life. It is a chance to talk about learning, discipline and growth.

The parallel reading section includes On the Life of Man and The World Is Too Much with Us. The fill-in-the-blanks activity asks students to compare Shakespeare's view of life with other poetic visions of human existence and nature.

Visible lines from the source: "What is our life? A play of passion" and "The world is too much with us; late and soon".

blocks.text: For this poem, remember the seven stages, the central metaphor of the stage, and the key phrases for each age.
